questionBank.stem: The speaker’s discussion of the room, staff time, and cabinet in paragraph 2 primarily reflects which feature of the rhetorical situation?
options: The speaker is seeking payment for previously donated labor.
The audience must decide whether the workshop merits institutional resources.
The audience has requested instruction in repairing household objects.
The speaker must explain why the workshop has already closed.
rationales: The speaker discusses resources, not personal compensation.
The board’s resource decision explains the response to costs.
The address requests continuation, not technical training.
Continuation is under consideration; closure has not occurred.

questionBank.stem: In paragraph 1, the account of the radio chiefly prepares the audience to consider
options: personal attachment as a reason to repair every object.
age as the best measure of an object’s worth.
learning as part of the workshop’s value.
speed as the workshop’s principal advantage.
rationales: The final sentence explicitly rejects saving every object.
The speaker does not rank objects by age.
The visitor participates in diagnosis, introducing learning beyond the repair count.
No comparison of repair speed is offered.

questionBank.stem: Which circumstance most directly prompts the writer’s argument?
options: Residents have demanded that all privately owned trees be removed.
Volunteers have proved that the shorter clinic route is unsafe in every season.
The city has stopped recording the condition of its trees.
A tree inventory may be used to make decisions about people’s access to shade.
rationales: Private trees illustrate inaccessible shade, not a removal demand.
The observations are limited to four clear days at noon.
The inventory remains useful for maintenance.
The essay challenges a mismatch between the measure and the decision.

questionBank.stem: The writer’s acknowledgment of residents’ care for mature trees in paragraph 4 indicates awareness that some readers may
options: interpret new priorities as a dismissal of their previous efforts.
regard volunteer observations as more reliable than any official record.
believe the district contains no trees worth preserving.
prefer a complete ban on planting additional trees.
rationales: The acknowledgment addresses a fear that existing care will be disregarded.
The concern is recognition of mature trees, not source hierarchy.
The residents value existing trees rather than deny their worth.
The passage gives no evidence of a blanket opposition to planting.

questionBank.stem: The writer’s role as an archivist most clearly shapes the passage through the writer’s
options: insistence that donors accept the archive’s existing labels.
examination of institutional choices in producing the collection.
claim to remember the night market better than its traders.
attempt to establish that professional records are always complete.
rationales: The project invites corrections to existing labels.
The writer examines forms, hours, storage, and selection decisions from inside the institution.
The writer does not claim firsthand market experience.
The final paragraph explicitly acknowledges incompleteness.

questionBank.stem: The passage is primarily intended to encourage donors and historians to
options: treat every refusal to contribute as evidence of historical neglect.
replace written records with a single shared oral history.
examine how collection practices shape the historical record.
judge the market’s importance by the number of surviving objects.
rationales: The writer protects refusal rather than assigning it one explanation.
Different sources and disagreements remain distinct.
The conclusion asks readers to inspect selection as well as retained materials.
The opening challenges precisely this inference from surviving records.

questionBank.stem: The student’s question in paragraph 2 provides the occasion for the writer to
options: argue that dictionaries have become unnecessary.
show that the student misunderstands the meaning of the disputed word.
establish that informal language belongs in every setting.
reconsider how judgments about usage should be made.
rationales: The conclusion retains a role for dictionaries.
The actual word and the student’s definition are not supplied.
The paragraph distinguishes what works in different settings.
The question opens an inquiry into context, conventions, and useful standards.

questionBank.stem: The writer’s use of a family anecdote most clearly establishes a speaker who
options: combines respect for linguistic authority with experience of its limits.
seeks to preserve every local expression against any change.
regards personal memory as sufficient proof of a language rule.
possesses professional authority because a relative compiled dictionaries.
rationales: The grandfather consults and questions the dictionary, modeling the essay’s stance.
The writer does not advocate preserving every expression.
Paragraph 5 explicitly limits what the anecdote proves.
The grandfather uses dictionaries; he does not compile them.

questionBank.stem: The neighbor’s question leads the writer to revise the proposal because it reveals that the writer had
options: assumed replacement lamps would cost less than existing fixtures.
neglected a practical concern central to another user of the street.
underestimated the association’s interest in astronomical photography.
failed to establish the neighbor’s knowledge of constellations.
rationales: No cost comparison is mentioned.
The question exposes the need for a clear, usable route home.
Photography is contrasted with the practical question, not requested by the association.
The neighbor’s relevant concern is walking home, not astronomy knowledge.

questionBank.stem: Which choice best describes the action the writer seeks from the association?
options: Immediate removal of streetlights to restore the view of the sky.
A photographic survey that replaces residents’ observations.
A permanent lighting standard based only on residents’ reported comfort.
A limited lighting trial evaluated through several users’ needs.
rationales: The writer explicitly retains illumination where needed.
The opening exposes the photograph’s limits as evidence.
Comfort alone is insufficient, and the trial does not justify a universal standard.
Paragraphs 4–5 propose a bounded trial with multiple measures and revision.

questionBank.stem: By calling the board’s resource questions “fair” in paragraph 2, the speaker primarily
options: implies that the board has already agreed to continue the workshop.
suggests that budget concerns should be set aside as irrelevant.
recognizes the audience’s stewardship responsibilities before broadening the evaluation.
concedes that the workshop costs more than its benefits justify.
rationales: The concluding request shows the decision remains open.
The speaker treats costs as legitimate rather than irrelevant.
The acknowledgment respects resource concerns while adding learning outcomes.
A fair question does not establish a negative answer.

questionBank.stem: The statement “I have bought a new kettle myself” in paragraph 3 most directly helps the speaker
options: demonstrate expertise in comparing appliance manufacturers.
distance the workshop from people who value old possessions.
establish that replacing an object is always cheaper than repair.
avoid presenting the workshop as a test of personal purity.
rationales: No brands or comparative expertise are offered.
The speaker retains respect for repair while rejecting absolutism.
The passage describes varied decisions, not a universal cost rule.
The admission counters a rigid anti-purchase sermon and makes the limits credible.

questionBank.stem: The description of the walk to the clinic appeals to readers chiefly by
options: connecting a technical inventory to an ordinary practical need.
portraying private gardeners as deliberately indifferent to their neighbors.
replacing the need for measurement with an emotional anecdote.
suggesting that medical appointments should determine all city spending.
rationales: The route makes the difference between tree count and usable shade concrete.
The writer does not attribute hostile motives to gardeners.
The passage calls for better measures, not abandoning measurement.
The clinic is an example, not a universal budget priority.

questionBank.stem: The acknowledgment that saplings do not create next summer’s shade is likely to reassure skeptical readers because it
options: indicates that mature trees should be moved to bus stops.
shows that the writer recognizes a practical limit of the preferred intervention.
proves that planting has no place in a long-term plan.
suggests that immediate relief is less important than accurate inventories.
rationales: Relocating mature trees is not proposed.
The limitation leads to interim measures rather than an unrealistic promise.
Planting remains part of the longer-term response.
The paragraph prioritizes usable relief and supplements planting.

questionBank.stem: In paragraph 2, the details about forms, hours, and storage chiefly appeal to readers’ willingness to
options: assume that an attractive collection is necessarily representative.
accept that practical constraints excuse every gap in a collection.
reconsider apparently neutral institutional routines as consequential choices.
rank archival work above the experiences of people who donate.
rationales: The essay repeatedly resists completeness inferred from appearance.
The writer makes choices examinable, not automatically excusable.
Ordinary routines reveal how the institution shapes what survives.
The passage invites contributors’ knowledge and corrections.

questionBank.stem: The discussion of contributors who decline in paragraph 4 strengthens the writer’s credibility primarily by
options: showing that the archive can verify memories without participation.
establishing that restricted materials are more reliable than public ones.
implying that the missing contributors have nothing valuable to offer.
acknowledging that collecting evidence does not override contributors’ agency.
rationales: Declining leaves gaps; independent verification is not claimed.
Access restrictions concern permission, not automatic reliability.
The writer refuses to interpret refusal as absence of value.
The distinction between invitation and consent limits the institution’s authority.

questionBank.stem: The writer’s observation that shared conventions make demanding thought possible is most likely intended to
options: find common ground with readers who fear that flexibility means abandoning standards.
suggest that readers should tolerate any difficulty caused by a writer.
establish that all communities already share identical conventions.
concede that new usages should be prohibited until officially approved.
rationales: The writer affirms a purpose for rules before arguing they can be revised.
Conventions reduce unnecessary reconstruction rather than excuse it.
The essay emphasizes differing relationships and contexts.
The next sentences allow revision without requiring prior official approval.

questionBank.stem: The image of a dictionary that need not “lock the door” invites readers to value
options: a return to the grandfather’s dictionary as a final authority.
shared standards that remain open to justified change.
private expression that requires no attention to readers.
a language whose meanings never depend on conventions.
rationales: The grandfather himself supplements the dictionary.
The image combines a shared room with openness, matching the balanced argument.
The essay repeatedly asks who understands a usage.
Conventions remain necessary for demanding thought.

questionBank.stem: The writer’s statement that the neighbor’s concern is “not a failure of imagination” primarily
options: establishes that immediate needs always outweigh every long-term goal.
suggests that artistic appreciation is irrelevant to public decisions.
protects a competing priority from being dismissed as narrow-minded.
implies that the neighbor shares the writer’s desire to observe stars.
rationales: The proposal coordinates needs rather than imposing a universal ranking.
The writer still values the stars and seeks accommodation.
The writer grants legitimacy to the practical use of the street.
The text does not assign the neighbor an astronomical interest.

questionBank.stem: The closing sentence most directly appeals to the association’s interest in
options: a compromise that gives every street identical fixtures.
a unanimous preference for the same lighting conditions.
a fair process that evaluates a shared space through multiple perspectives.
expert control over decisions residents cannot understand.
rationales: Different patterns of use caution against uniform application.
The passage acknowledges persistent differences rather than requiring unanimity.
Shared measures extend the essay’s recognition of different street users.
Residents’ reports are central to the proposed evaluation.

questionBank.stem: Which opening sentence would best establish the problem that the proposed trial addresses?
options: The directors will soon consider how to divide next year’s funds among several visitor programs.
Our museum’s oldest maps were donated by families who hoped visitors would study them closely.
Visitor questions often go unrecorded because our comment desk stands near only one exit.
Museums can make difficult subjects accessible through exhibits that combine objects with written explanations.
rationales: The meeting context alone gives no reason the trial is needed.
Donation history does not establish the feedback problem.
This opening identifies the feedback gap developed in sentences 4–6.
The general praise does not prepare the specific proposal.

questionBank.stem: Which sentence would best follow sentence 15 to conclude by emphasizing the trial’s limited but useful purpose?
options: If the trial succeeds, the museum will no longer need staff to explain its exhibits.
Many other museums have also experimented with ways to welcome visitors.
The museum should eventually invite visitors to vote on every acquisition.
A small trial cannot tell us what every visitor thinks, but it can show where a clearer explanation is needed.
rationales: It overstates what feedback can replace.
The general comparison supplies no culminating implication.
Acquisitions are outside the proposed purpose.
The sentence returns to useful label improvements while respecting the trial’s limits.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants the introduction to connect the opening image to the exchange’s educational purpose. Which sentence should follow sentence 1?
options: Growing notes can preserve experience alongside the seeds.
An exchange can bring gardeners together at regular meetings.
Locally saved seeds may be unfamiliar to new gardeners.
Packets also make it easier to store small seeds.
rationales: The notes connect the packet image to the educational purpose.
Meeting together does not explain what the packet can preserve.
Unfamiliarity introduces a problem without making the requested connection.
Storage develops a physical benefit rather than the learning claim.

questionBank.stem: Which conclusion would best reinforce the draft’s qualified recommendation?
options: The committee’s primary task should be to increase the town’s overall population.
Begin small, record problems, and let the first season’s experience determine whether the exchange should grow.
Because seeds are inexpensive, the committee should immediately accept every variety.
Gardening requires patience, a virtue that all people should cultivate.
rationales: Population growth has no basis in the argument.
The conclusion unites the pilot, evaluation, and conditional expansion.
It ignores the stated labeling and disease concerns.
The broad moral does not follow from the proposed decision.

questionBank.stem: Which opening would most effectively frame the competing needs developed in the draft?
options: The history of our street begins long before its current shops opened.
Noise is among the most common topics of conversation in modern life.
A street can be ready for business before some of its residents are ready to wake.
Every business on our street follows exactly the same morning routine.
rationales: Historical context does not prepare the scheduling argument.
The broad claim is less specific to the proposed conflict.
It introduces the conflict between business preparation and residents’ sleep.
The draft explicitly shows differences among businesses.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 14 with an ending that identifies a constructive next step. Which choice best achieves this goal?
options: Require every resident and shopkeeper to approve the same permanent schedule today.
Postpone discussion until the association can guarantee that no one will be inconvenienced.
Choose the schedule preferred by whichever group submits more comments.
Agree on a trial and a review date, then use both sets of records to decide what should change.
rationales: Permanent unanimity exceeds the limited trial.
The draft proposes learning under imperfect conditions, not waiting for certainty.
Counting comments replaces the proposed evaluation of consequences.
This follows the evidence-gathering process and preserves revision.

questionBank.stem: Which introductory sentence would best prepare readers for the proposal’s focus on usable information?
options: A repair may end before a visitor’s questions do.
A repaired object may remain useful for several more years.
A volunteer may learn as much as the visitor.
A workshop can bring neighbors together around a practical task.
rationales: The opening establishes the need for explanations after the repair.
Longevity concerns repair outcomes rather than instructions.
Volunteer learning does not frame visitors’ need for later guidance.
Community connection is relevant broadly but does not introduce the information problem.

questionBank.stem: Which ending would best connect the proposed reader test to the draft’s central purpose?
options: A consistent sheet gives every visitor the same information in the same amount of space.
A useful sheet helps a visitor decide what to do after the volunteer is gone.
A detailed sheet preserves a record of every tool the volunteer used during the repair.
An attractive sheet reminds a visitor that the workshop is a welcoming place to return.
rationales: Uniform detail conflicts with the layered response to differing needs.
Independent decision-making connects the reader test to the governing purpose.
Tool inventories may record work without helping the next decision.
A welcoming impression does not establish actionable usability.

questionBank.stem: Which opening would best introduce the need for the proposed notebook?
options: People often enjoy looking at pictures from the past.
Digital photographs generally take up less physical space than printed ones.
A photograph can survive intact while the names and circumstances needed to understand it disappear.
Our historical society has existed for many decades.
rationales: Enjoyment alone does not prepare the evidentiary purpose.
Storage capacity is not the proposal’s central problem.
It establishes the gap between preserved images and missing context.
Institutional age does not explain the need.

questionBank.stem: Which sentence would best follow sentence 15 as a conclusion?
options: Its value would lie in allowing contributors to bypass every form of review.
Its value would lie in replacing uncertainty with a single story approved by the society.
Its value would lie in showing how we know, where accounts differ, and what still needs investigation.
Its value would lie chiefly in attracting more online visitors than neighboring organizations.
rationales: The proposal explicitly includes moderation and review.
A single certain story contradicts preserved disagreement.
This extends the concern with inspectable evidence and retained uncertainty.
Popularity is not the draft’s stated criterion.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants to address directors concerned about staff workload. Which addition after sentence 10 would be most useful?
options: A summary of favorable comments could show staff that visitors appreciate their work.
A photograph of the comment station could show where volunteers might welcome visitors.
An end-of-year report could display the total number of notes the museum received.
A short review checklist could make the weekly task more predictable.
rationales: Appreciation does not establish the time required.
The station’s appearance does not explain the review process.
A later total does not clarify the weekly burden.
A defined process addresses the directors’ workload concern.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants sentence 13 to address visitors who cannot comfortably use a phone. Which revision best accomplishes this goal?
options: Visitors could use paper forms with clear print, with the same questions offered in an accessible digital version.
Visitors could ask another visitor to enter every response for them.
Visitors could submit comments only after creating an online account.
Visitors could use the digital form because most people now own phones.
rationales: Equivalent paper access directly addresses the specified need.
Mandatory reliance on strangers reduces independent access.
An account adds a barrier rather than addressing it.
Ownership does not establish comfortable use.

questionBank.stem: Which addition would best address inexperienced gardeners’ need to understand sentence 3?
options: A cabinet diagram could show where users should return packets after reading the labels.
A sample label could show a plant name, date, and note such as “afternoon shade.”
A donor list could identify gardeners who have contributed seeds in several previous seasons.
A calendar could show when gardeners usually begin preparing their plots for the growing season.
rationales: Cabinet navigation does not clarify what the label must say.
The example makes the required fields intelligible to a novice.
Donor experience does not explain the fields themselves.
Seasonal timing does not explain the required source information.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants to reassure cautious committee members without promising complete safety. Which replacement for sentence 11 best achieves this goal?
options: Because experienced gardeners understand plants, the exchange would require no review.
These precautions would ensure that every seed grows successfully in every plot.
These precautions could reduce identifiable risks, while the pilot’s records would help the committee detect recurring problems.
The committee should avoid mentioning risks because doing so may discourage participation.
rationales: Experience does not remove the need for review.
It makes an unsupported universal guarantee.
It acknowledges limits and explains how monitoring supports a decision.
Concealment does not responsibly address the audience’s concern.

questionBank.stem: Which addition would best show understanding of shopkeepers whose suppliers control delivery times?
options: The association could describe all exceptions as evidence of unwillingness to cooperate.
The association could publish photographs of the street’s historic storefronts.
Residents could choose the delivery schedules without consulting suppliers.
The trial could allow documented exceptions while recording how often supplier schedules prevent participation.
rationales: It misrepresents a scheduling constraint as motive.
Photographs do not address the concern.
It ignores the authority suppliers hold over timing.
The addition addresses an actual constraint without abandoning evaluation.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants instructions for residents to produce useful reports rather than general approval ratings. Which revision of sentence 11 best serves that goal?
options: Residents should note the time, duration, and kind of interruption, without recording identifying details about individuals.
Residents should repeat their preferred schedule in each daily entry.
Residents should report only interruptions that confirm the trial is working.
Residents should indicate whether they generally like the shops on the street.
rationales: Specific observations serve the evaluation and avoid unnecessary identifying information.
Repeated preferences do not document outcomes.
Selective reporting would bias the evidence.
General liking does not measure the trial’s effects.

questionBank.stem: Which revision of sentence 5 best adapts the instructions for readers unfamiliar with repair terminology?
options: Volunteers should omit the names of parts whenever those names are unfamiliar.
Volunteers should use familiar words and briefly define any technical term needed to identify a part.
Volunteers should replace every familiar word with a specialist’s preferred term.
Volunteers should assume readers can locate definitions elsewhere.
rationales: Omitting necessary names can make instructions unusable.
The revision balances precision with the reader’s need for explanation.
Specialist language increases the barrier.
External lookup does not meet the stated audience need.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants to address readers who need different levels of detail. Which choice best develops sentences 8–9?
options: The second page could introduce different safety instructions from the first.
The writer could combine every detail into one unbroken paragraph.
The first page could state the essential action, with clearly labeled references to optional explanations on the second.
The workshop could give the shorter sheet only to visitors who appear experienced.
rationales: Conflicting instructions would undermine clarity and safety.
An unbroken paragraph makes selective reading difficult.

questionBank.stem: Which addition would best put the interview accounts into conversation with the survey’s measure?
options: A count of reading days leaves open how a student finds time within each day.
The interviews show that the survey’s numerical responses must all be false.
The interviews should be combined into a single quotation spoken by both students.
A count of days proves that every day offers students equal uninterrupted time.
rationales: The sentence identifies a question the interviews can illuminate without claiming population prevalence.
Different evidentiary contributions do not establish false responses.
That would erase distinct sources and misattribute wording.
The interviews suggest differing circumstances.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants to compare the librarian’s hypothesis with the interviews. Which sentence is most useful?
options: The students refute the librarian because their interviews contain no discussion of newsletters.
Interest may influence participation; circumstances may influence the reported behavior.
The librarian and students all prove that buying journals increases response rates.
The librarian’s explanation and the students’ experiences are identical kinds of statistical measurements.
rationales: Silence on recruitment does not refute a recruitment hypothesis.
The sentence distinguishes a possible recruitment effect from conditions of behavior.
None of the accounts establishes that claim.
They are different forms of qualitative contribution, not equivalent statistical measures.

questionBank.stem: Which question would best help the writer move beyond listing the sources one after another?
options: Which source can be omitted so that no disagreement remains?
Which source has the most impressive-sounding title?
What does each source explain that the others leave unresolved?
How can the sources be made to appear unanimous?
rationales: Avoiding difference is not the same as analyzing it.
A title does not establish an argumentative relationship.
This directs attention to complementary roles and gaps in the argument.
Forced agreement could erase genuine differences in scope or claim.

questionBank.stem: Which sentence best introduces a tension between the advertisement and the rest of the article?
options: All sources use numbers to measure the journal’s effect on reading.
The advertisement proves that the survey asked the wrong students.
The advertisement and interviews disagree about the school’s enrollment.
The advertisement guarantees an outcome; the other sources leave explanatory questions open.
rationales: The interviews and advertisement provide no such shared measure.
It supplies no evidence about respondent selection.
No such disagreement appears.
This identifies the difference in certainty and evidentiary role.

questionBank.stem: Which sentence best integrates the survey result into a claim with an appropriate scope?
options: The library found that fifty students read every day throughout the year.
Among the eighty volunteers who responded, fifty reported reading on at least three days in the previous week.
Fifty students prove that the entire school reads on most days every week.
Eighty students were observed reading on fifty different days.
rationales: The survey concerns at least three days in one previous week.
The sentence keeps the denominator, self-report, threshold, and time frame visible.
The claim generalizes beyond respondents and changes the measure.
This reverses and misrepresents the reported quantities.

questionBank.stem: Which version most effectively introduces the bus-travel account as an example rather than population evidence?
options: The interview suggests that bus travel is the main explanation for the survey’s reported frequency.
Students read because buses provide every respondent with uninterrupted time.
One interviewee’s reading during bus travel illustrates a condition the survey omitted.
The survey proved that bus travel causes reading habits to become permanent.
rationales: One student’s account does not establish the dominant explanation among respondents.
The generalization exceeds one interview and ignores differing conditions.
The framing attributes the experience and identifies its limited explanatory role.
No causal test or lasting-habit measure appears.

questionBank.stem: Which addition after the sibling-care account would best explain its relevance?
options: The account establishes that students with siblings never enjoy reading.
The account shows that the library newsletter caused the student’s responsibilities.
The account proves that every survey answer should be replaced with an interview.
The account cautions against treating fewer reported reading days as direct evidence of weaker interest.
rationales: The statement turns a constraint into an unsupported universal preference.
No such causal relation is established.
Different evidence types can contribute without one universally replacing the other.
Time constraints offer a reason that frequency and motivation may diverge.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants to quote the advertisement’s guarantee without endorsing it. Which framing is best?
options: The advertised “lasting reading habit” lacks a definition and comparison evidence.
The students said that the journal provides a “lasting reading habit.”
“Lasting reading habit” proves that the product’s buyers all read daily.
A “lasting reading habit” is guaranteed, as the article’s evidence has demonstrated.
rationales: The quotation is attributed and evaluated in relation to the missing support.
The quotation belongs to the advertisement, not the interviewees.
The quoted phrase alone does not establish measured behavior.
The article has not demonstrated the guarantee.

questionBank.stem: Which sentence best connects the proposed year-group sample to the earlier evidence?
options: Sampling across year groups would erase the need to record nonresponse.
Sampling across year groups could improve coverage beyond voluntary newsletter recruitment.
Sampling across year groups would prove the advertised journal works.
Sampling across year groups would make every interview account typical.
rationales: The response rate would still matter.
The sentence explains why the proposal responds to the original method.
A broader descriptive sample does not test that product’s effect.
A sampling plan does not make individual stories representative automatically.

questionBank.stem: A student wants to integrate the ledger into an argument about duration. Which choice best preserves the distinction between record and inference?
options: The ledger must be ignored because its later entries complicate the preferred account.
The ledger records a permanent eight-hour day because the anniversary article uses that phrase.
Three eight-hour weeks followed by ten-hour days challenge the article’s claim of permanence.
The ledger proves that the workers felt no benefit during the three weeks.
rationales: Complicating evidence should be interpreted rather than discarded.
This gives the article’s claim to a source that contradicts it.
The evidence is stated before its specific implication is explained.
The entries do not measure their feelings.

questionBank.stem: Which framing most responsibly introduces the supervisor’s letter?
options: The historian proved that every early arrival was voluntary leisure.
The anniversary article measured the precise duration of the early wait.
The worker admitted that no unpaid work had ever occurred.
The supervisor attributed early gate opening to sheltering first-train arrivals.
rationales: The letter does not establish that universal conclusion.
The later commemoration is not that measurement.
This transfers a claim to the wrong source and overstates it.
The verb and attribution preserve the statement as the supervisor’s explanation.

questionBank.stem: Which commentary would best follow a quotation from the worker describing the early wait?
options: The described wait leaves activity before payable hours to be investigated.
The quotation’s vividness makes the payroll entries unnecessary.
The account proves that the supervisor’s letter cannot contain any accurate detail.
The account settles the experience of every worker across the factory’s entire history.
rationales: This explains both the value and the limit of the quoted experience.
Vividness does not replace evidence answering a different question.
Compatible facts may have different explanations.
That generalization exceeds a single morning’s account.

questionBank.stem: Which revision best prevents the historian’s interpretation from being presented as the ledger’s own statement?
options: The ledger argues that the worker’s memory is unreliable.
The ledger lists payable hours; I infer that arrival time must be investigated through additional records.
The ledger says that all historians should distrust every payroll.
The ledger explains the supervisor’s private motives.
rationales: The ledger records hours rather than evaluating a later interpretation.
The revision separates the entry’s content from the historian’s methodological conclusion.
The record does not voice that methodological rule.
The entries do not establish those motives.

questionBank.stem: Which numerical statement is supported by the draft?
options: Eighty percent of students bought a reading journal in the previous week.
Fifty of eighty respondents reported reading on at least three days in the previous week.
Fifty percent of all eight hundred students read every day.
Three quarters of the school responded to the library survey.
rationales: The survey did not measure journal purchases.
This preserves the actual sample, threshold, and interval.
The denominator, percentage, and frequency claim are all changed.
Eighty of eight hundred is one tenth, not three quarters.

questionBank.stem: What is the most important problem with using the fifty responses to support the schoolwide conclusion in paragraph 1?
options: The fifty respondents must have misunderstood the question because fifty is not half of eighty.
The survey result becomes invalid whenever any number is expressed in words.
Neither schoolwide representation nor reading on most days follows from these responses.
The school is too small for any numerical description to be useful.
rationales: A proportion other than one half does not indicate misunderstanding.
Presentation form does not determine validity.
Both the population and the frequency claim exceed the reported result.
A school of eight hundred can be studied; the issue is the method and inference.

questionBank.stem: If the writer adds the percentage 62.5%, which wording gives it a defensible meaning?
options: The survey proves that 62.5% of all school reading occurs on buses.
The school’s reading rate rose 62.5% over the previous year.
The journal increased each respondent’s reading by 62.5%.
Of the respondents, 62.5% reported reading on at least three days in the previous week.
rationales: Neither the denominator nor the behavior matches the measure.
No earlier-year baseline appears.
No before-and-after product comparison was conducted.
Fifty divided by eighty is 62.5%, and the wording retains the sample’s scope.

questionBank.stem: The unchanged number of paid workers during the three eight-hour weeks most directly helps the reader distinguish
options: a change in recorded hours from a change in the recorded workforce count
a permanent policy from every possible temporary exception
a reduction in unpaid labor from a reduction in commuting time
an increase in wages from a decrease in the price of goods
rationales: The two quantities are separately described.
Duration still requires the later ledger entries.
The ledger does not directly measure either quantity.
Neither wages nor prices is supplied.

questionBank.stem: Which conclusion would require evidence beyond the ledger figures reported in paragraph 4?
options: The number of paid workers remained unchanged during those weeks.
Workers received the same total pay during the shorter weeks.
Recorded daily hours fell from ten to eight for three weeks.
Later entries again recorded ten-hour days.
rationales: That is explicitly reported.
The passage gives hours and worker count, not wage rates or total earnings.
That is explicitly reported.
That is explicitly reported.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants a chart caption that prevents a misleading population inference. Which choice is best?
options: The effect of buying a journal on every student’s reading frequency.
Reading habits of all 800 students, measured without exception.
Responses from 80 voluntary library-newsletter participants; results are not a schoolwide estimate.
Proof that most students read daily throughout the school year.
rationales: The survey did not test the product.
The survey did not cover all students.
The caption identifies recruitment and the limit of generalization.
The threshold and time frame are unsupported.

questionBank.stem: The phrase “make agreement where none has yet been established” presents careless synthesis as
options: the construction of an apparent consensus rather than the discovery of an evidenced one
a physical rearrangement that changes the dates written in the ledger
a necessary courtesy owed to the factory’s proprietor
the inevitable result of comparing any two historical documents
rationales: The writer warns against treating shared subject matter as confirmation.
The change is interpretive rather than material.
The historian prioritizes evidence rather than ceremonial agreement.
Careful comparison remains the essay’s method.

questionBank.stem: The metaphor of a “boundary” between source record and interpretation chiefly emphasizes
options: the physical edge of a damaged ledger page
the need to make an inference distinguishable and traceable to its evidence
a prohibition on drawing any inference from historical material
a division that prevents sources from being considered together
rationales: The boundary concerns kinds of claim, not page condition.
Citation allows readers to inspect where the historian’s contribution begins.
The essay interprets sources while marking the limit.
The essay brings them into relation without merging their scopes.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants an analogy that clarifies the survey’s limited coverage without dismissing its results. Which choice is best?
options: The responses are a verdict proving which students care about books.
The responses are a broken clock that can never indicate anything.
The responses are a window onto one group, not a census of the whole school.
The responses are a mirror in which every student appears equally clearly.
rationales: The survey does not establish motivation or moral worth.
This dismisses the usable respondent data entirely.
The analogy preserves a useful partial view and distinguishes comprehensive coverage.
This implies representation the method does not establish.

questionBank.stem: Which analogy would best explain why interviews and a frequency survey can contribute different information?
options: A tally and an account are interchangeable rulers that always give the same measurement.
A survey is a lock that prevents any explanation from entering.
An interview is a certificate that automatically makes a small survey representative.
A tally counts entries; an account explains obstacles to entering.
rationales: This erases their different contributions.
The survey leaves explanatory questions open rather than prohibiting them.
The analogy grants an evidentiary power interviews do not have.
The comparison distinguishes frequency from contextual conditions without making either sufficient for all questions.

questionBank.stem: The writer proposes calling the advertised journal “a guaranteed engine of reading.” Which revision would better match the evidence?
options: The journal is a proposed aid whose effect the advertisement has not demonstrated.
The journal is a cure for all possible obstacles to reading.
The journal is proof that time and circumstances never affect habits.
The journal is an engine that drives every student at the same speed.
rationales: The revision removes a causal guarantee unsupported by the reported evidence.
This extends the guarantee beyond the evidence.
The interviews suggest that circumstances deserve inquiry.
This intensifies the unsupported universal effect.

questionBank.stem: Which figurative closing would best connect the results to further investigation?
options: These responses are a wall beyond which no useful research can proceed.
These responses begin an inquiry; they do not finish judging the school.
These responses close the book on every student’s motivation.
These responses crown the bookseller’s product as the only solution.
rationales: The draft explicitly proposes a follow-up.
The metaphor treats limited findings as grounds for inquiry rather than a final verdict.
This claims finality and a measure the survey does not provide.
No evidence establishes the product’s effect or exclusivity.

questionBank.stem: According to the final paragraph, citation contributes to reasoning by
options: guaranteeing that any conclusion accompanied by a reference is correct
proving that quoted wording is more reliable than every paraphrase
making it unnecessary to explain differences among sources
allowing readers to inspect the relation between a source’s record and the historian’s inference
rationales: A reference makes a claim traceable but does not validate every inference.
Reliability depends on source and use, not quotation alone.
The essay requires those differences to be interpreted.
Its function extends beyond naming the place a sentence came from.

questionBank.stem: A student writes, “The ledger establishes that the workers welcomed the shorter day.” What would a citation to the ledger fail to supply?
options: Evidence of workers’ reactions to the change.
A basis for identifying the temporary reduction.
A way to compare earlier and later recorded hours.
The recorded number of hours during the three weeks.
rationales: Hours and workforce count do not measure welcome or satisfaction.
The entries establish the reported reduction.
The ledger permits that comparison.
The ledger does supply that information.

questionBank.stem: Which statement most needs attribution to the anniversary article rather than to the ledger?
options: Later ledger pages return to ten-hour days.
The shorter day marked the beginning of a permanent improvement.
The ledger records eight-hour days for three weeks.
The number of paid workers remains the same during the shorter weeks.
rationales: This also comes from the ledger.
That interpretation belongs to the anniversary article and is challenged by later ledger entries.
This is a report of the ledger’s entries.
That quantitative observation is drawn from the ledger.

questionBank.stem: Why would placing one citation after a paragraph combining all three sources sometimes be insufficiently clear?
options: A citation is useful only when all sources agree.
A paragraph may never discuss more than one source.
Readers might be unable to tell which source supports each claim.
Every sentence must quote the source’s exact wording.
rationales: Attribution is especially useful when their contributions differ.
Synthesis often requires several sources in one paragraph.
Distinct records and interpretations require traceable attribution.
Paraphrase and commentary are legitimate when clearly attributed and supported.

questionBank.stem: Which revision most clearly attributes the proposed selection explanation?
options: It is known that all newsletter readers are the most interested students.
The survey suggested that newsletter readers might already be especially interested in books.
The survey proved that each student read the newsletter because of a lasting habit.
The librarian suggested that newsletter readers might already be especially interested in books.
rationales: The revision removes attribution and overstates the claim.
The explanation is attributed to the librarian, not established by the survey itself.
The survey did not measure that reason.
The wording names the speaker and retains the suggestion’s tentative status.

questionBank.stem: The writer paraphrases the sibling-care interview without quoting it. Which practice best preserves responsible attribution?
options: Identify the account as one interviewee’s experience and distinguish it from the article’s interpretation.
Present the experience as something the writer personally observed in every household.
Attribute it to the librarian because the librarian also appears in the article.
Omit attribution because no exact words have been retained.
rationales: Paraphrasing changes wording but does not erase the source of the experience.
That changes both source and scope without evidence.
A nearby source cannot be substituted for the actual speaker.
The underlying account still comes from a source.

questionBank.stem: Which sentence most clearly separates a reported finding from the writer’s proposed next step?
options: Eighty responses establish that sampling across year groups will produce a representative result.
The survey received eighty responses; I propose sampling across year groups in a follow-up.
The survey proposed a sample across year groups after receiving eighty responses.
A year-group sample produced eighty responses to the original survey.
rationales: The current count cannot guarantee the representativeness of a proposed method.
The syntax distinguishes the existing result from the author’s recommendation.
This gives the writer’s proposed next step to the survey as though it were a reported recommendation.
This incorrectly describes the original voluntary newsletter recruitment.

questionBank.stem: The writer encountered the advertisement through an article that quoted it, rather than viewing the advertisement itself. Which revision would be most transparent?
options: Remove quotation marks but keep the exact phrase without attribution.
Describe the advertisement’s full layout as if personally examined.
Identify the article as the place where the quoted advertisement was encountered.
Attribute the advertisement’s guarantee to the interviewed student.
rationales: Changing punctuation does not make another source’s wording original.
That would claim access the writer did not have.
This avoids implying direct inspection of a source the writer has not seen.
This gives the statement to the wrong source.

questionBank.stem: Which source information would most help a reader check the claim about the eighty responses?
options: A reference only to the school’s current sports schedule.
A note that the number eighty seems plausible to the writer.
A citation to the advertisement’s product slogan.
A reference to the survey report, including its collection period and recruitment method.
rationales: That source does not document the survey.
Plausibility is not traceable support.
The advertisement does not establish the school’s response count.
Those details identify the evidence and clarify its scope.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants to retain the advertisement’s wording “guarantees a lasting reading habit.” Which choice best handles it?
options: Attribute the phrase to all survey respondents collectively.
Quote and attribute the phrase, then explain the missing evidence for the guarantee.
Use the phrase as the article’s own conclusion without naming its source.
Quote the phrase but change “guarantees” to “sometimes” without marking the alteration.
rationales: The survey did not ask them to make that claim.
This preserves ownership of wording and evaluates its support.
That conceals the borrowed language and endorses an unsupported claim.
That would misrepresent the source’s actual level of certainty.

questionBank.stem: For a question about how the factory was remembered forty years later, the anniversary article functions most directly as
options: a complete substitute for the worker’s personal account
primary evidence of the commemorative portrayal at that later time
a direct measurement of every worker’s earlier arrival time
a source with no possible evidentiary use because it is retrospective
rationales: The sources answer different questions.
Its own language records that public act of remembering.
It does not measure those events.
Retrospection is itself relevant to a question about memory.

questionBank.stem: For a question about the payroll’s recorded hours, which source is most direct?
options: A modern visitor’s impression of the factory building.
The anniversary article’s praise of the proprietor.
The ledger entries for the relevant weeks.
The historian’s favorite analogy for public memory.
rationales: An impression of the building does not establish recorded hours.
It offers a later interpretation rather than the direct payroll entries.
They record the payable hours under investigation.
An analogy does not supply payroll data.

questionBank.stem: The distinction between a primary and a secondary use of a source depends in this passage chiefly on
options: whether the source has a longer title than the other documents
whether the source contains numbers rather than prose
whether the historian agrees with the source’s conclusion
the question being asked and the source’s relation to that question
rationales: Title length does not determine evidentiary relation.
Both numbers and prose can function as direct evidence for appropriate questions.
Agreement does not define primary or secondary status.
A retrospective article can be direct evidence of commemoration while requiring corroboration for earlier hours.

questionBank.stem: Which statement about the historian’s essay is best supported?
options: It interprets earlier records and makes the grounds of that interpretation available for scrutiny.
It eliminates the need for readers to examine the cited sources.
It proves that a source created near an event is reliable for every possible question.
It becomes the original payroll because it reproduces some figures.
rationales: The essay synthesizes documents while distinguishing record from inference.
The conclusion explicitly values returning to them.
The worker’s letter remains limited in representativeness.
Reproducing data does not make an interpretation the original record.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants direct evidence of what the survey asked. Which addition would be most useful?
options: The librarian’s recollection of what the survey was intended to discover.
The actual survey question and the response options presented to students.
A later advertisement about reading journals.
A student’s explanation of why a particular answer was selected.
rationales: An account of intention is less direct evidence of exact wording than the instrument itself.
Those materials directly establish the measure’s wording.
That advertisement does not document the survey instrument.
An individual interpretation does not establish all the question and response wording.

questionBank.stem: Which use of the advertisement would be most defensible without accepting its guarantee?
options: Treat it as a transcript of the sibling-care interview.
Treat it as a controlled experiment demonstrating the journal’s effect.
Treat it as evidence of how the bookseller markets the journal.
Treat it as the source of the school’s enrollment figure.
rationales: It is a different source with a different purpose.
The draft reports no comparison group or outcome definition.
Its wording directly shows the commercial claim being made.
The advertisement does not supply that school-specific information.

questionBank.stem: A later article summarizes the school survey. What would consulting the original survey report chiefly help the writer do?
options: Guarantee that every student answered truthfully.
Avoid considering the original report’s own limitations.
Prove that any later interpretation must be false.
Check whether the summary preserves the measure, recruitment, and scope of the original result.
rationales: The report cannot guarantee each respondent’s honesty.
Direct access permits evaluation; it does not remove limitations.
Later interpretations can be accurate when faithful to evidence.
The original can clarify details lost or altered in summary.

questionBank.stem: Which addition would best distinguish a student’s direct account from the writer’s broader inference?
options: A personal constraint suggests a broader question about reading opportunities.
The article’s inference makes the interview a schoolwide experiment.
The student’s direct experience means no other evidence can be relevant.
The interviewee has measured every family’s schedule.
rationales: The sentence separates individual evidence from a question for broader investigation.
Interpretation does not change the source’s method.
Other sources can test prevalence and alternative explanations.
That claim exceeds the reported personal account.

questionBank.stem: Which summary most accurately captures the historian’s central argument?
options: Citation guarantees that a historian’s interpretation is beyond dispute.
The oldest source should always replace every later account.
Compare sources through their purposes and limits, not presumed agreement.
Personal letters are useful only when they agree with payroll records.
rationales: Citation permits scrutiny rather than preventing it.
The essay uses later memory as evidence for an appropriate question.
This includes both comparison and the discipline of limiting claims.
The differences can themselves become subjects for inquiry.

questionBank.stem: Which paraphrase preserves the point of the discussion of early gate opening?
options: The supervisor proved that no worker ever performed unpaid work.
The two letters cannot be compared because one describes a gate.
The worker’s letter proves that every minute before dawn was paid.
An alternative explanation complicates unpaid-work claims without disproving them.
rationales: That universal conclusion is explicitly rejected.
Their shared event invites comparison with attention to perspective.
The letter does not establish pay for each minute.
This retains both the complication and the remaining uncertainty.

questionBank.stem: Which summary of the three-week change is most faithful to paragraph 4?
options: The reduction may matter even though it was temporary.
The reduction was permanent because the anniversary article celebrated it.
The historian knows that workers disliked the shorter day.
The reduction never occurred because it did not last forever.
rationales: The summary preserves significance while limiting duration.
Later ledger entries challenge that claim.
No such reaction is established.
Temporary occurrence is still occurrence.

questionBank.stem: Which summary of the survey is most accurate and concise?
options: A controlled study proved that journals create permanent habits.
Eighty newsletter volunteers described recent reading; schoolwide frequency remains unestablished.
The school measured every student’s daily reading for a year.
Eighty students were interviewed about why they disliked assigned books.
rationales: The survey did not test that intervention.
The summary preserves recruitment, subject, and scope.
Coverage, interval, and method are all misstated.
The reported survey asked frequency outside assigned work, not that motive.

questionBank.stem: Which paraphrase of the two interviews avoids adding an unsupported judgment?
options: The second student proved that reading is impossible in every household with children.
One student cared about books, while the other preferred caring for siblings.
Travel provided one student reading time; family duties constrained another’s.
Both students said that a purchased journal solved their scheduling problems.
rationales: The generalization exceeds one account.
The accounts do not establish that contrast of preferences.
This preserves the reported circumstances without ranking motivation.
Neither account reports that solution.

questionBank.stem: The writer wants to shorten the advertisement discussion while preserving its evidentiary problem. Which choice is best?
options: The advertisement mentions a journal that people can buy.
The advertisement is false because advertisements are short.
The advertisement proves that every buyer becomes a daily reader.
The advertisement guarantees a lasting habit without reporting how that outcome was defined or compared.
rationales: This omits the guarantee and the reason it needs scrutiny.
Length does not establish truth or falsity.
The revision endorses the unsupported claim.
The revision retains the claim and the missing methodological support.

questionBank.stem: Which paraphrase best preserves the qualification in sentence 10?
options: The interviews suggest possible conditions but do not show how widespread those conditions are.
The interviews cannot suggest anything because only two students spoke.
The interviews show that circumstances never influence reading.
The interviews establish the exact percentage of students facing each condition.
rationales: This retains the difference between illustration and prevalence.
Limited accounts can suggest questions without measuring frequency.
The accounts invite inquiry into circumstances.
No prevalence measure is supplied.

questionBank.stem: Which summary would best serve as a brief introduction to the proposed follow-up?
options: The current survey proves that year groups have identical reading patterns.
The current survey leaves questions about representation that a broader sampling plan could investigate.
The current survey has settled every question except the journal’s price.
The current survey means that another study would necessarily reach the same result.
rationales: No such group comparison is reported.
The sentence connects the new plan to an identified limitation.
It leaves representation and interpretation unresolved.
A follow-up could yield different findings.

questionBank.stem: Which revision of “They do not justify ranking every student’s motivation” preserves its meaning?
options: The results cannot describe how respondents answered the frequency question.
The results prove that no student is motivated to read.
Reported reading days do not fully measure individual motivation.
The results establish a reliable ranking of every student’s character.
rationales: The survey can describe responses within its limited scope.
This turns a limit on inference into an unsupported negative claim.
The revision explains the prohibited inference without denying all value in the results.
This asserts the very overreach the sentence rejects.

questionBank.stem: The statement “That gap does not prove that anyone would object” qualifies the argument by
options: conceding that the archive’s possession settles every question of later use
suggesting that the writer no longer regards consent as relevant
establishing that everyone pictured has already approved the poster
distinguishing an absence of documented agreement from evidence of actual opposition
rationales: The next sentence rejects that inference.
The essay continues to recommend inquiry and careful choices.
The record does not contain every person’s wishes.
The writer refuses to turn unknown wishes into a claim of known objection.

questionBank.stem: The writer’s acknowledgment that a complete reconstruction of wishes may be impossible chiefly
options: limits the demand for certainty while retaining the value of partial inquiry
makes the association’s celebratory purpose sufficient evidence of agreement
establishes that the two deceased participants opposed the event
withdraws every proposed action until all uncertainty disappears
rationales: The practical recommendation asks what can be learned and what remains unresolved.
A worthwhile purpose does not supply missing consent.
Their wishes are not established by their deaths.
The passage offers several feasible actions despite incomplete knowledge.

questionBank.stem: The phrase “still requires careful decisions” in paragraph 4 qualifies the proposed contextual display by
options: proving that a contextual display circulates more widely than a poster
preventing the alternative format from appearing to eliminate responsibility
showing that the writer rejects the alternative before considering its purpose
suggesting that only posters can raise concerns about representation
rationales: The paragraph contrasts wide circulation with an explanatory setting.
The display changes the communicative setting but does not settle every ethical question.
The writer identifies a useful distinction while retaining care.
The qualification explicitly extends concern to the display.

questionBank.stem: Which revision to sentence 3 would best qualify the benefit of sharing while preserving support for the proposal?
options: Sharing should replace all private ownership of household equipment.
Sharing will eliminate every purchase once the shelf opens.
Sharing could reduce some purchases of tools that residents need only occasionally.
Sharing has no possible benefit because some tools require specialist instruction.
rationales: The broader prescription exceeds the limited proposal.
The universal guarantee remains unsupported.
The revision narrows both certainty and scope to the proposal’s relevant use.
The initial collection can exclude those tools without losing every benefit.

questionBank.stem: Which version of sentence 6 best expresses what the interest survey warrants?
options: The responses establish precisely how often each tool will be borrowed.
The responses are irrelevant unless every center visitor answered.
The responses require the committee to purchase a complete workshop immediately.
Expressed interest warrants exploration, while demand and maintenance remain untested.
rationales: The survey asked interest, not actual frequency.
A limited voluntary sample can inform exploration when its limits remain explicit.
The evidence does not warrant that scale or obligation.
The wording preserves a planning implication without predicting measured use.

questionBank.stem: Which addition would best qualify the one-term proposal without making it indecisive?
options: Continue only if observed use justifies the maintenance work.
Cancel the collection if any person asks a question about a tool.
Expand the collection because a longer shelf will appear more successful.
Continue the collection regardless of what the review finds.
rationales: The condition links continuation to the stated evaluation criteria.
This imposes an arbitrary condition unrelated to feasibility.
Appearance does not establish reliable operation.
This removes the role of evaluation.

questionBank.stem: The concern that seeking agreement may delay the event is treated as
options: evidence that all pictured participants have consented
a practical objection that deserves a workable response
proof that members raising the concern oppose shared memory
an objection the writer answers by promising complete certainty
rationales: A scheduling concern does not establish agreement.
The writer acknowledges difficulty and proposes partial inquiry and another image.
The writer does not assign that hostile motive.
The response explicitly accepts that complete reconstruction may be impossible.

questionBank.stem: Which response most accurately describes how the writer addresses the difficulty of contacting everyone?
options: The difficulty proves that the original photograph should be destroyed.

questionBank.stem: Which revision best calibrates a claim about the proposed format’s likely benefit?

The format will make missed deadlines impossible forever.

questionBank.stem: Which statement best captures the writer’s central position?

Let technical experts settle the bell’s future because material preservation determines appropriate use.
rationales: The writer recommends repair and occasional ringing despite unresolved disagreement.
The proposal combines repair, contextual recollections, limited ringing, and an explanation of remaining losses.
The writer distinguishes attention from repetition and rejects daily ringing as an automatic consequence.

questionBank.stem: The distinction between repair and ringing is essential to the argument because

The passage supplies no such technical finding.

questionBank.stem: The writer’s proposed occasional ringing is best understood as

a temporary technical test required before returning to the old daily schedule
a choice whose losses must be justified rather than a solution claimed to satisfy everyone
rationales: The passage explicitly rejects that description.
The justification concerns explained occasions and present claims, not arithmetic alone.

options: Responses about how announced occasions affect nearby activities and what purposes those occasions serve.

rationales: This bears on the proposal’s stated use, explanation, and present consequences.

Recognition alone does not settle how its sound affects current users.

questionBank.stem: Which thesis best fits the notice’s purpose of inviting useful deliberation?
options: The current parking count proves that every resident will benefit from replacing the spaces.
Judge effects on different uses and explain the resulting choice.
The most attractive drawing should determine whether the proposal is adopted.
The number of supportive messages should be the only criterion for approval.
rationales: The count does not establish all needs or future seat use.
The claim connects evidence, competing needs, and accountable choice.
Appearance does not establish the consequences the notice asks residents to examine.

questionBank.stem: Which revision to sentence 3 would establish a defensible position without excluding disagreement?
options: Residents should reject the plan because any change creates some cost.
Residents who oppose the change should explain why they do not care about the town.
Residents can support the town while disagreeing about which arrangement best serves its uses.

rationales: The presence of a cost does not by itself settle the balance of reasons.

The existence of a drawing does not establish merit.

questionBank.stem: Which addition would best connect the examples of parking and waiting to the recommendation in sentence 10?
options: The examples show that only people who drive use the square for practical reasons.

rationales: Waiting on foot is also presented as a practical use.

questionBank.stem: Which conclusion follows most reasonably from the invitation to comment?
options: Specific accounts of effects can improve the reasons for retaining, revising, or rejecting the proposal.
The council can avoid explaining its decision if comments disagree.
The proposal becomes correct as soon as every drawing is labeled.

rationales: The request seeks evidence and suggested changes relevant to the decision.

questionBank.stem: The two opening memories complicate “our shared memory” by

rationales: The proposal includes conflicting recollections beside the repaired object.

questionBank.stem: The reference to the night worker and the quiet class adds complexity by

identifying two groups whose preferences are necessarily identical
showing that technical repair is impossible in a community building
introducing present claims that historical attachment alone cannot resolve
rationales: Their memories remain relevant to repair and interpretation.
Both are relevant examples, but the passage does not equate all their preferences.
The committee has already established repair feasibility.
The current setting has users affected by morning ringing.

options: identifies something each simplified account leaves out
avoids recommending any action until the sides agree
concludes that every argument is equally supported
assigns exactly equal numerical weight to every statement
rationales: Discipline-only descriptions omit pleasure, while hostility-to-history descriptions omit the preservation/use distinction.
The writer makes a concrete proposal despite disagreement.
The writer evaluates mischaracterizations and proposes reasons for a choice.
The essay supplies no numerical weighting method.

preserves the cost of the proposal within the argument for adopting it
shows that the writer has abandoned the proposal

The sentence identifies potentially simultaneous benefits and costs.
The passage identifies different uses and needs.

questionBank.stem: Which revision would best acknowledge uncertainty without preventing a recommendation?
options: The counts are limited, so no decision about the square can ever be justified.

questionBank.stem: Which concluding qualification would best support a complex but definite decision?
options: List every uncertainty without explaining any choice.

rationales: That avoids the decision and its reasons.

The proposal includes conflicting recollections.

Civic concern can motivate disagreement about the effects of a design.

options: An unlabeled decorative view paired with a demand for unconditional approval.
